prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "COSTCO WHOLESALE CORP /NEW" (ticker COST), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "COST", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Costco Wholesale Corporation
markets: US and Canadian warehouse club retail
Household goods, electronics and general merchandise
Gasoline, pharmacy, optical and other warehouse services
International warehouse clubs (Mexico, Japan, UK, Korea, Australia, Taiwan, China, Europe)

mission.statement: To continually provide our members with quality goods and services at the lowest possible prices.
mission.source: Costco Code of Ethics (company website and annual report materials)
mission.plain: Costco exists to give its members good-quality things at the lowest prices it can.

about.plain: Costco runs giant warehouse stores where people pay a yearly fee to shop. Inside, it sells a small choice of food, drinks, TVs, tyres and household items in big packs at very low prices. It keeps prices low by adding only a small markup and makes much of its profit from the membership fees. It has 939 warehouses in 14 countries and about 84 million paying members.
about.customers: Families and small businesses that pay a yearly membership fee to shop there.
about.everyday: The Costco warehouse with the $1.50 hot dog and soda combo, cheap petrol and huge packs of Kirkland Signature paper towels.

money.plain: food, fresh meat and produce, drinks, cleaning and paper goods, electronics, clothes and home goods

money.part: Gas stations, pharmacy, optical and other warehouse services
money.plain: petrol, medicines, glasses, hearing aids, food court and travel; sales up 20% in FY2026
$65 Gold Star and Executive membership fees, $5.9B in FY2026 and the bulk of profit
Costco.com, app orders and delivery; about 11% of FY2026 net sales and growing about 20% a year
ads shown to members using Costco's shopper data, launched in 2024

result.summary: Costco has a wide moat built on a self-reinforcing loop: huge volume on only about 4,000 items gives it buying scale, it caps markups so prices are lowest, and that keeps 84.1 million paying members renewing at 92.3% in the US and Canada, whose $5.9B of fees fund the low prices. Rivals such as Sam's Club and BJ's copy the format but not its scale, culture or member trust, and Costco's earnings have compounded steadily for decades.

pricingPower.evidence: Costco deliberately does not use pricing power on goods (gross margin on net sales held at 11.09% in FY2026 versus 11.13% in FY2021), but its membership fee shows real pricing power: after raising the US/Canada fee from $60 to $65 in September 2024, renewal rates stayed at 92.3% in the US and Canada and paid members still grew 3.8% to 84.1 million, with membership fee income up 11% to $5,907M in FY2026.

moats.evidence: Costco and its Kirkland Signature private label are trusted symbols of value and quality; management says Kirkland items save members 15% to 20% versus national brands, and Costco topped the 2024 ACSI grocery ranking with a score of 85.
The prepaid annual fee and Executive members' 2% reward (42.3 million Executive members, up 9.4%) encourage consolidating spending at Costco, though members can still shop elsewhere freely.
More members give Costco more buying power and lower prices for everyone, an indirect scale loop rather than a true network effect between users.

With $297.2B of FY2026 net sales concentrated on roughly 4,000 SKUs, each item sells in enormous volume, letting Costco run on an 11.09% gross margin and SG&A of about 9% of sales that conventional retailers cannot match.
A warehouse club needs a large membership base per location, so many US markets only support one or two clubs, and Costco usually holds the best sites.
Its policy of capping markups (about 14% for branded and 15% for Kirkland items) and earning profit from fees is hard for margin-driven supermarket chains to copy without wrecking their own profits.

Decades of disciplined merchandising, a cross-dock depot supply chain, low-cost warehouse operations and a culture of passing savings to members have been studied for years but not replicated at its productivity.
Its main exclusive assets are the Kirkland Signature brand and a loyal, long-tenured workforce of about 355,000, not an irreplaceable resource.

customers.evidence: Renewal rates of 92.3% in the US and Canada and 89.8% worldwide at fiscal year-end 2026, paid members up 3.8% to 84.1 million, and a 2024 ACSI score of 85 (tied for top among grocers, ahead of Sam's Club at 83 and Walmart at 74).

talent.evidence: Costco pays well above retail norms (in 2025 it announced raises taking most US store workers above $30 an hour), promotes heavily from within (CEO Ron Vachris started as a forklift driver) and is known for low staff turnover among about 355,000 employees.

product.evidence: Its offer of low prices on high-quality bulk goods, Kirkland Signature private label, cheap gasoline (members saved an estimated $3.2B at the pump in FY2026) and a generous return policy is widely seen as the best value in retail.

threats: Sam's Club's investment in technology (Scan & Go, no-checkout exits) and new clubs, plus BJ's expansion, narrowing Costco's lead in the club format
Amazon, Walmart+ and fast grocery delivery reducing the need for bulk trips to a warehouse
Tariffs and inflation squeezing its thin 11% gross margin, since it refuses to pass on much of the cost
Rising wage and benefit costs for about 355,000 employees, including Teamsters-represented workers
Saturation of the best US sites, making growth depend more on international markets where execution is harder
A rich valuation (about 46 times FY2026 earnings) that leaves little room for any slowdown
Culture dilution as founder-era leaders retire and the company grows larger

ceo.name: Ron Vachris
ceo.background: Joined Price Club (Costco's predecessor) as a forklift driver in 1982 while studying business at Glendale Community College; rose through warehouse management, regional VP, head of merchandising and President/COO (2022) before becoming CEO on January 1, 2024

c1.evidence: Costco is the world's leading warehouse club with $303.2B of FY2026 revenue, but grocery and general retail is a mature industry, not an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Members choose it for the lowest prices on quality goods, Kirkland Signature and trust in its capped markups, a scale-and-culture advantage that Sam's Club and BJ's have not matched in four decades.

c3.evidence: Costco is a household name and the default warehouse club in the US, and members recommend it widely, reflected in a 2024 ACSI score of 85 and 92.3% US/Canada renewal.

c4.evidence: Its mission of quality goods at the lowest possible prices and code of ethics (obey the law, take care of members and employees, respect suppliers, reward shareholders) are emphasised constantly, but the mission is about value for money rather than transforming the world.

c6.evidence: “bulk, cheap, quality, hot dog, Kirkland” - the public impression is overwhelmingly positive, with Costco seen as a fair, member-friendly company that treats its workers well.

c7.evidence: Its addressable market of global grocery and general merchandise is in the trillions of dollars, but it grows slowly; Costco gains share through value-seeking and its digitally-enabled sales growing about 20% a year rather than riding a fast secular trend.

c8.evidence: It plans 33 openings in FY2027 and targets 30 net new warehouses a year, with room in China, Europe, Japan and Australia, plus newer areas such as retail media and e-commerce, but it stays within warehouse retail.

m1.evidence: Vachris has a clear plan (faster warehouse openings, better technology such as scan-and-go checkout, digital growth) but he is a disciplined steward of Jim Sinegal's model rather than a futurist.

m2.evidence: A 40-plus-year company lifer who started as a forklift driver, Vachris acts like a founder-steward, prioritising long-term member value over quarterly profit.

m4.evidence: He leads by Costco's code to take care of members and employees, backing above-market pay raises in 2025 and visiting warehouses frequently.

m5.evidence: Costco's culture is strong and distinctive, but it is built on operational discipline and value rather than inventing new products or technologies.

m6.evidence: Vachris is deeply hands-on in merchandising and operations (he previously ran merchandising) but has no engineering background.

m7.evidence: Costco under Vachris kept its employee-first pay, resisted pressure to drop its diversity policies in January 2025 and keeps markups capped, showing priorities beyond short-term profit.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Ron Vachris at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university could be found.

m8b.evidence: Vachris is a low-profile operator who rarely gives interviews, unlike flamboyant founder-CEOs.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2024, revenue grew from $254.5B (FY2024) to $303.2B (FY2026) and net income from $7.4B to $9.2B, with record membership and renewal rates.

m10.evidence: Costco is famous for frugality: modest Issaquah headquarters, almost no advertising, executive pay far below peers' and Jim Sinegal's era of a small office and no frills.

c10.evidence: It saves money for 84.1 million paying members (150.4 million cardholders) in 14 countries, a large benefit, though it improves budgets rather than transforming lives.

p2.evidence: Running a $300B retailer on an 11% gross margin is very hard to copy and useful for household budgets, but retailing is not technologically difficult.

f1.evidence: Total revenue rose every year from $195.9B in FY2021 to $227.0B, $242.3B, $254.5B, $275.2B and $303.2B in FY2026.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 3.42% in FY2021 to 3.85% in FY2026, while gross margin on net sales was flat at 11.13% versus 11.09%, by design.

f3.evidence: At August 30, 2026 total debt of $6.2B was far below cash and short-term investments of $21.3B and FY2026 operating cash flow of $15.8B, with total equity of $35.8B.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose every year from $6,708M in FY2021 to $11,685M in FY2026, and operating cash flow reached $15,825M in FY2026, up from $13,335M in FY2025.

v1.evidence: For an ordinary shopper the reason is simple: low prices on good-quality bulk goods and gas, with a no-quibble return policy, which is why 92.3% of US and Canadian members renew.

v2.evidence: Costco regularly ranks high on employer lists such as Forbes' America's Best Large Employers and is known for above-market pay and benefits, low turnover and promotion from within.

c5.evidence: If Costco disappeared, tens of millions of families and small businesses would pay more for groceries, gas and household goods and lose their most trusted value retailer, and well-paid employees would lose good jobs.
